item.title: Everyone’s Using This A.I. Dictation App That I Want to Murder With a Hammer
item.description:
I haven’t written a single word of this. Well, I guess I have technically quote-unquote written this in that I am the author of the words. But I haven’t touched the keyboard. The words you’re reading appeared here on this page from my voice. I spoke them, and they immediately and accurately appeared? This feels like a magician’s trick, or like I’m some kind of 1940s Don Draper type with an army of transcriptionists in my employ.

I’m using an app called Wispr Flow, an A.I. voice-to-text app. According to the tech bros on X and Reddit, it is a key to sharing their genius with the world by unshackling them from the need to type, as well as a tool that will unlock the full force of human civilization. Reid Hoffman and Marc Andreessen use this. Why? Wispr Flow claims an extremely high degree of accuracy, and also that by using it, people can write four times faster than they write with their hands.

Although I’m actually not sure how A.I. is involved in this. I just went to another tab and spoke into the search box: “How is A.I. involved in the app Wispr Flow?” And it told me the answer is that the software’s A.I. can handle natural speech and convert it correctly really well in real time, even if you’re doing something complicated like writing a play with multiple layers of dialogue or vibe coding a project on GitHub.

I’m looking at the paragraphs above and I’m really itching to edit them. A lot of these sentences are bad. But the whole point of Wispr Flow is that you don’t edit. You speak naturally and organically. You CAN double back in your speech. For instance, you can say to Wispr Flow, “Delete that last word,” and it will do it for you pretty seamlessly. But you can’t tell it to take this sentence and put it there, or to go back and change that preposition above, or to reorder some of your paragraphs so that the argument has a more logical flow. You can’t tell it to make you sound smarter, or at least not yet. (Note from this story’s editor: The magazine has made light tweaks out of pity for the reader and writer alike. Also, our writers do not use A.I. tools to write articles except when specifically testing them for articles about such technology.)

In the past, when I’ve tried to use dictation features on my iPhone while walking or holding too many objects in my hands, it’s abysmal. I’ll speak a Slack message to my boss like “I’m running late to the meeting” and that little wheel will spin for several seconds and then it will straight up convert the text into something like “I absolutely loathe you and never want to see you again!”

In contrast to all that, Wispr Flow’s speed and accuracy are pretty astonishing. You can quite literally whisper to it at the softest possible volume, like I’m doing right now, and the transcript will be almost perfect. When you set up the app on your computer or phone, you can also tailor the way it renders your speech for specific contexts as well. So for instance, you could have it type out all your emails with capital letters and exclamation points and all your texts in lowercase with no commas. It’ll cut out all the filler words in your speech, such as “like” and “um,” if you want it to, or you can choose to leave those in by selecting a casual tone. Wow. Earlier it wrote down the words “quote-unquote” and now it’s already doing actual quote marks. I guess that tracks, because one of the things the app told me when I set it up was that it would learn from my voice and start to analyze my common speech patterns.

If I start to speak a list, it will understand it’s a list. The things I need to do this morning are:

● Buy bananas

● Write this article

● Learn how to endure the sound of my own voice

For a year or so now I have seen Wispr Flow praised by M.B.A. types online, but what caught my eye enough for me to try it out myself was an article from Bloomberg in May reporting that the start-up was in funding talks for a $2 billion valuation — $2 billion! Just to save people a few minutes and carpal tunnel! Can you add a link to the Bloomberg piece, Wispr Flow? I guess not. (Note from this story’s editor: The link is here.)

I’m reading these paragraphs above again now and I think I sound like an idiot?

To tell you the truth, I hate this. I hate Wispr Flow so much. I hate that so many people in the world are lauding this like it’s the greatest invention, when actually I think it’s making everyone sound a little like an idiot, and now everybody has to read everyone else’s idiot words. I wish I could describe elegantly how much I hate it with some kind of handy, clever metaphor, but that kind of creativity comes to me through writing with my hands.

Because writing, when it comes down to it, is a higher form of thinking. Writing takes time and editing and a deep level of commitment. Writing is a rigorous process to understand your own thoughts and then lay those thoughts out in a way that convinces or inspires or moves other people. But speaking is not that process. Speaking out loud can be tremendously useful when you need to deliver instructions or talk something out with another person or jot down a quick brainstorm while you are in the middle of washing your face in the bathroom or something.

We’ve been talking a lot about the so-called end of literacy, but the real problem isn’t that people don’t read — it’s that they do read and spend all day ferociously consuming words, but those words aren’t really written, not in the way that any writer would consider them written, because the words they’re reading are more like speaking. I wish I could italicize the word “really” in that last sentence. Italics really. Uh. Close enough, I guess.

I just got a notification from Wispr Flow congratulating me that I have written enough words with the software in just these few minutes here that I have “written 12 wedding vows.” Which, I mean, is kind of my point. Can you imagine if wedding vows were off-the-cuff speaking? Could we stop, soon, with the apps and programs that want to replace every facet of human thought with something more efficient, like there’s no value at all in … reflection? At this point I’m ready never to speak aloud ever again.

It’s a few days later, and my editor has just read this draft and informed me that my first paragraph is factually incorrect: Don Draper is famously a 1960s man. That’s really embarrassing, and all I can say is thank goodness for people.

item.title: Status Defines Friendship for Too Many Americans
item.description:
Why do I feel like I’m being sold friends?

Join a “modern social club,” one ad beckons. “Turn strangers into friends” via curated dinner parties at trendy restaurants. A luxury condo building flogs its “community clubhouse” as an exciting amenity, while yet another social start-up informs me, rather ominously, that “we find your people.”

It’s possible that my feeds are too well primed: the algorithms can tell that I’m in my 30s, living in a city known for its transience, and that I frequently search for data on and read stories about our changing social lives. But the sheer number of these ads suggests that the need for friendship is widespread enough that an industry is forming around it.

There are the run clubs and exercise “cults.” On Instagram, I was seduced by a vibey post reminiscing about the pre-cellphone era of house parties. After I swiped through a carousel of nostalgia-inducing pictures, I was invited to just that kind of gathering — for a fee.

The loneliness epidemic has been well publicized, from the last surgeon general’s repeated warnings to musings in major media outlets. And the loneliness market has boomed: Venture capital firms are investing in “social and relational health”; technologists are selling companions and chatbots as cures for isolation; politicians and philanthropists have adopted “belonging” as a buzzword.

Even though I’d still love to make new friends, I’m lucky to already be embedded in a tight-knit group dating back to college. And these for-profit solutions all seem pitched at those who need them the least — socializing positioned as a luxury good. If isolation really is a societywide crisis, we need societywide solutions — and an understanding of who has been left out most acutely from what friendship promises.

In pursuit of that aim, the researchers Sam Pressler, a fellow at the University of Virginia’s Karsh Institute of Democracy, and Soren Duggan, a communications strategist and Army veteran with a background in human intelligence collection, produced a report this spring titled “Nobody to Call,” based on a series of 30 in-depth, qualitative interviews with men ranging from their mid-20s to their mid-40s without college degrees. They hoped to add texture to the conversation on loneliness by seeking out those who they believe are struggling the most. We’ve all experienced social atrophy, Mr. Pressler told me, but for men without degrees the bottom has fallen out.

College completion rates have risen over the decades for both men and women, but a growing proportion of those who aren’t graduating are men. As of 2021, men made up around 43 percent of four-year-college enrollees, down from approximately 57 percent in 1970. “As the college degree has increasingly become the great sorting function in American life,” Pressler and Duggan write, “men without degrees have increasingly found themselves sorted out.” We tend to talk about the loneliness crisis in terms of gender, but class, as derived from educational status, is the factor too touchy — or too invisible — to acknowledge.

Less than half of Americans hold bachelor’s degrees, but those without are less likely to have places to gather (parks, libraries, even coffee shops), are less likely to join civic groups or social clubs and report having far fewer close friends or people to turn to for social support. The four-year degree isn’t just an economic signal; it’s become a lifestyle determinant.

In the “Nobody to Call” case studies and interview transcripts, men without college degrees described social drift that turns into a social cliff: Graduating from high school meant the loss of an accessible infrastructure for connection, and with it a whittling down of peer groups, and no new structure — college, the military, a union, churches or civic groups — to take its place.

And while higher education is often discussed in terms of its economic value, its relational value is strangely overlooked. The multiyear college experience brings together groups of peers who transition into adulthood together, often forming lasting bonds in the process and connecting to mentors and institutions along the way.

The majority of the men Pressler and Duggan interviewed were almost completely disconnected; of the 30, almost half reported having no close friends, and six reported having only one. In one of many poignant lines from the report, one interviewee noted bluntly: “I don’t have anybody that I feel like I matter to.”

Friendships, purpose and opportunity are built over time, through institutions and shared settings. For many men, unstable work — transient gig jobs, uncontrollable schedules — allows only for the creation of tenuous, easily breakable ties. A lack of money, time and affordable places to gather adds to a lack of confidence and social know-how, making new relationships harder to form or sustain. As one interviewee put it: “It is not community when you exclude people that don’t have them jobs like you, the money like you or even look like you.”

Most of the men interviewed as part of “Nobody to Call” seemed to deeply want to connect and contribute to their broader communities (contrary to the common public narrative of nihilistic, misogynistic loners actively contributing to a “male loneliness crisis”), but material barriers, compounding into psychological ones, often kept them from doing so.

Many admitted that although they wanted to build community and make friends, they had little sense of where to start. “I don’t know how to just go out in the wild and pick up friends. People don’t do as many in-person things as they used to many years ago.”

But there are examples of civic leaders making it easier. For instance, as part of the 2026 FIFA World Cup celebrations, New York City’s office of the mayor opened five public soccer pitches around the city for overnight pickup games — an initiative called NYC Open Play. It was free, available at nontraditional hours and staffed to encourage connection; thousands joined to play.

There are other brass-tacks policy changes that could help: ending just-in-time scheduling, providing more job support and protections for gig workers and putting in place better leave policies that might allow space for the development of one’s civic life. But a major issue is simply being seen and understood — not as statistics or caricatures, but as members of a shared community.

America is overdue for a reckoning with how we have made college the main rite of passage to cultural life while letting others atrophy. Potential solutions to this could be anything from more support for apprenticeships and vocational programs — ones that impart the sense of belonging that can be achieved only through the shared pursuit of excellence — to the dream of a national service corps that pools young people together across economic lines.

Like many of America’s most pressing social crises, the loneliness epidemic is divided by class. The “loneliness industry” seeks to capitalize on the crisis of social isolation via paid solutions like those hawked to me online, but friendship as a pay-to-play luxury will continue to leave broad swaths of Americans out.

If loneliness really is a public health crisis, it’s the responsibility of government and institutions, not just the market, to begin offering solutions. Connection is, or at least should be, a public good.

Christine Emba is the author of “Rethinking Sex: A Provocation” and a senior fellow at the American Enterprise Institute.

item.title: They Were Paying Their Student Loans. Then the Rules Changed.
item.description:
Imagine for a moment that your bank changed the terms of a loan that you had been paying down for more than a decade. It informs you that it is increasing your payment and extending the term by five years.

Any commercial bank would most likely be accused of violating basic contract law.

So what happens when the federal government does it?

As part of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act passed last summer, Congress rewrote the rules for certain student loans. Since legislators are permitted to make changes, borrowers’ legal rights aren’t clear-cut — but to many of them, it still feels a lot like a broken contract.

The big tax and policy bill overhauled the federal student loan machinery, from borrowing limits to repayment plans. But instead of applying only to new borrowers, certain changes have swept in many holders of existing loans. They include a less noticed group who will need to choose a new income-driven repayment plan with more onerous terms than a program they could have signed up for as many as 14 years ago.

Matthew Hansen, a 40-year-old pharmacist from Sandy, Utah, who borrowed $166,000 for graduate school, is among them. “It feels like your mortgage lender calling you and saying, ‘Hey, your home is worth a lot more now, and so we’re going to add five years and $100,000 to your mortgage,’” he said.

In 2013, Dr. Hansen enrolled in the income-driven Pay as You Earn repayment plan, known as PAYE, in which borrowers pay 10 percent of their discretionary income for 20 years. After that, any debt remaining is discharged. But the policy bill will eliminate PAYE from the menu of repayment options in the summer of 2028, forcing Dr. Hansen to enroll in a plan with less favorable terms.

This appears to be the first time that the government has changed the terms of income-driven repayment plans so that existing borrowers are generally worse off, according to borrower advocates and legal experts.

“Congress really pulled the rug out from under them by abruptly increasing their financial obligations after the fact, and as borrowers realize this they are shocked and furious,” said Abby Shafroth, director of the National Consumer Law Center’s Student Loan Borrower Assistance Project. “I’m sympathetic to Congress’s desire to simplify student loan repayment options, but this was the wrong way to do it.”

The policy bill is phasing out at least a half-dozen repayment plans — including the Biden-era Save as You Earn (SAVE) program, which two Republican-led states challenged in court — and replacing them with two new ones.

Borrowers who are enrolled in PAYE, like Dr. Hansen, generally have two options. They can enroll in the Repayment Assistance Plan (RAP), a new income-driven program with a 30-year term — a decade longer than PAYE. Or they can move into Income-Based Repayment, known as I.B.R., an existing program that will remain open to borrowers (who do not take out new federal student loans).

Enrolling in I.B.R. would increase Dr. Hansen’s payments to 15 percent of his discretionary income from 10 percent, and extend his term to 25 years from 20. That version of I.B.R. is available to people who took out loans before July 1, 2014.

But a more favorable version of I.B.R. is open to people who took out loans on or after July 1, 2014. They can pay 10 percent of their discretionary income toward their balance for 20 years, so their loan terms are largely the same as they were in PAYE.

For Dr. Hansen, it’s a significant difference. His current PAYE bill is $747 a month, he said, and with a baby on the way, it will drop to $647. But he’ll eventually owe $970 on the older I.B.R. plan. RAP would cost $1,009 monthly.

It’s not clear how many borrowers are affected. While PAYE recently had about 1.5 million enrollees, according to data from Federal Student Aid, it’s possible that some of them are eligible for the newer, similar version of I.B.R., Ms. Shafroth explained.

But it’s also possible that people in the Biden-era SAVE plan could be affected. If they took out loans on or after Oct. 1, 2011, and before July 1, 2014, they will be eligible only for the older I.B.R. plan (or RAP) with less favorable terms.

For Dominic Chaklos, 35, scholarships largely covered his undergraduate degree, but he borrowed the full cost of law school at Santa Clara University, where he graduated in 2015. He said he had taken out loans on the understanding that he’d be eligible for PAYE.

Mr. Chaklos, an entertainment lawyer in Los Angeles, said he had 10 years of PAYE payments remaining. He, too, will need to choose between the older version of I.B.R. and RAP.

“It just doesn’t make any sense that you can change the terms like that,” said Mr. Chaklos, who pays $1,500 a month and has made financial decisions — buying a home with his wife, having a child, paying for day care — with that payment in mind. “Thankfully, we have some buffer in our budget. But I’m sure there’s a lot more people that don’t — and even still, it’s obviously going to affect us.”

Federal student loans are contracts between the Education Department and borrowers, but the legal argument of those who feel the changes are unfair appears to fall in a gray area.

Mr. Chaklos’s promissory note says that the loan terms and conditions are determined by the Higher Education Act, which the One Big Beautiful Bill Act amended, and that any changes to the act that affect the terms will be applied to the loan.

“The promissory note doesn’t promise a specific repayment plan. It promises ‘a choice of several repayment plans,’” said Stanley Tate, a lawyer who represents student borrowers. “Congress reserved the right to change the menu, on the face of the document the borrower signed. I.B.R. and RAP both exist and both are income-based, so the generic promise is still being kept.”

But the new law breaks from past practice by eliminating programs for borrowers midstream, said Eileen Connor, president and executive director of the Project on Predatory Student Lending, a legal group that represents defrauded borrowers. She also pointed out that when borrowers took out their loans, they received loan counseling, which must provide information on the repayment options, including descriptions of the each plan’s features.

“Congress has in the past added new repayment programs and applied them to new loans, and limited existing repayment plans to those already in them,” she added. “Here, Congress has taken away a repayment plan from people enrolled in it, and replaced it with something that is definitionally less favorable.

“It did so without explanation, and so we don’t know whether the legal rights of current borrowers were considered at all or, if they were, what the analysis was.”

item.title: The Trump Administration Is Trying to Keep College Students From Voting. Don’t Let It.
item.description:
When America lowered the voting age from 21 to 18, the move had broad bipartisan support, starting with college students and civil rights groups and running right up through Congress and state legislatures. At the 26th Amendment’s signing ceremony, 55 years ago last month, President Richard Nixon declared that “America’s new voters, America’s young generation,” would bring “moral courage” and “a spirit of high idealism” to the country.

Today, however, America’s current “young generation” — and in particular, college students — stand at the intersection of two of the Trump administration’s favorite targets: voting rights and higher education. Through a range of measures, the administration has sought to make it more difficult for students to vote and for colleges and universities to assist student voters.

The connection between education and democracy has been core to American ideals since the nation’s founding. Thomas Jefferson, who went on to found the University of Virginia, wrote, “No other sure foundation can be devised, for the preservation of freedom and happiness.” For this historical reason — and more practically, because college students may live away from home — institutions of higher learning have traditionally made an effort to facilitate registration and voting.

The Trump administration’s new regulations are aimed right at those efforts. If universities do not fight to maintain the vital work they have done to promote democracy in its most literal form, they will lose that foundational purpose, and the nation will lose the vital contributions of countless young adults.

Last August, just as the academic year was beginning, the Department of Education sent a “Dear Colleague” letter to college administrators informing them that their institutions could no longer use federal work-study funds to support nonpartisan civic activities such as voter registration, voter hotlines and voter assistance at polling places. These are activities that groups such as the ALL IN Campus Democracy Challenge and the Students Learn Students Vote Coalition have shown demonstrably increase student voter turnout.

The message in the latest edition of the Federal Student Aid Handbook appears to set a somewhat less restrictive standard. So what exactly is permissible? The American Council on Education encourages institutions to “assess from their own risk vantage point.”

Helping students vote should not require nerves of steel.

New regulations that could go into effect as early as Oct. 1, just over a month before the 2026 midterms, would place even greater restrictions on this activity. The Office of Management and Budget has proposed to classify voter registration efforts by colleges and other nonprofit organizations, even if nonpartisan, as “lobbying,” and therefore to ban the use of any federal grant dollars for that purpose or “related activities.” We can only speculate about the rationale for this change, because the O.M.B. failed to provide the justification that is required by law.

The attacks on college-based voter registration efforts don’t just limit healthy democratic engagement; they violate the spirit of our existing federal law. The 1998 reauthorization of the Higher Education Act requires colleges and universities to make a “good faith” effort to provide their students with voter registration materials.

In addition, laws in states such as California, Maryland, Minnesota and Michigan require proactive measures to encourage student voting. Depending on how these new federal regulations are interpreted, they might come into conflict with the state laws, too.

In February, Secretary of Education Linda McMahon declared that “American colleges and universities should be focused on teaching, learning and research — not influencing elections.” Her statement was made in a news release about a federal investigation into the National Study of Learning, Voting and Engagement, a nonpartisan research project that for 13 years has helped educators understand and promote civic participation at more than 1,000 colleges and universities.

Neither the study nor Tufts, the study’s home, has been accused of any wrongdoing, but the threat of sanctions — against both the National Student Clearinghouse, the source of essential data for the study, and the schools that participate in the project — appears to have been enough to halt research for the foreseeable future.

The paradox is that Ms. McMahon, along with many other members of the Trump administration and a growing number of voices on both sides of the political divide, champions a return to civics education. But the purpose of that education does not end at the classroom door.

Its value is in its ability to get people involved in civic life and the democratic process. That’s precisely the goal of these college activities and organizations, yet they are coming under relentless attack.

American colleges and universities must not be neutral on the issues of democracy and civic participation. Institutions should do what they have been doing since before the Declaration of Independence: educate students and help shape them as informed and engaged citizens.

In the 2022 midterms, only 31.3 percent of college students voted. We should all view this as unacceptable. College leaders should articulate their opposition to the proposed rule changes and find resources to promote and defend the most foundational of democratic rights. This is not a question of partisanship but of citizenship.

This month, when first-year students arrived at Bard College, where for 15 years I have directed the Center for Civic Engagement, they all had to visit a voter registration booth even before they received their room keys. No one was required to register, but several hundred did, and those who were already registered and planning to vote from home received help with the often complex absentee ballot process.

Instead of shying away from this legitimate activity, colleges should redouble their efforts to reach young people, educate them and assist them as they navigate the registration and voting process. They should not just teach students about their democratic rights; they should help students realize them. There is no truer way to fulfill their educational mission.

Jonathan Becker is the acting president of Bard College and an editor of “Youth Voting Rights: Civil Rights, the Twenty-Sixth Amendment, and the Fight for American Democracy on College Campuses.”
